draft.title: Antiderivatives
card: An antiderivative of f(x) is a function whose derivative is f(x). Because a constant disappears when we differentiate, every antiderivative has + c.
Powers
∫xⁿ dx = xⁿ⁺¹/(n + 1) + c, for n ≠ −1. Add 1 to the power, then divide by the new power. For 1/x, ∫1/x dx = loge|x| + c.
Exponential
∫e^(kx) dx = (1/k)e^(kx) + c, for k ≠ 0. Divide by the number k in front of x.
Trig
∫sin(kx) dx = −(1/k)cos(kx) + c and ∫cos(kx) dx = (1/k)sin(kx) + c. Example: ∫cos(2x) dx = (1/2)sin(2x) + c.
draft.remember: Raise the power and divide, or divide by k, then always add c.

a.why: Add 1 to the power to get x³, then divide by 3: 6x³/3 = 2x³. Multiplying by 2 instead gives 12x, which is the derivative, not the antiderivative. Leaving out c is also incomplete.
a.clue: Raise the power by 1, then divide by the new power.

b.why: Integrate each term. e^(3x) gives (1/3)e^(3x), and sin(2x) gives −(1/2)cos(2x). The sign is negative because the derivative of cos is −sin. Multiplying by k instead of dividing is a common slip.
b.clue: Divide by k in each term, and check the sign for sin.

problems.detail: "Every antiderivative has + c" is loose. A single antiderivative such as 2x³ is a valid antiderivative without c. It is the general antiderivative (the indefinite integral) that carries + c. VCE questions asking for "an antiderivative" accept answers without c, so this wording could mislead students.

The why says "Multiplying by 2 instead gives 12x". Multiplying 6x² by 2 gives 12x², not 12x. The 12x distractor comes from differentiating: multiply by the power and lower it by 1. The explanation of this slip is confusing.

check.summary: The questions and keyed answers are correct. The card's claim that every antiderivative has + c is imprecise, since only the general antiderivative does. The why for (a) wrongly says multiplying by 2 gives 12x, when 12x comes from differentiating.

final.title: Antiderivatives
card: An antiderivative of \(f(x)\) is a function whose derivative is \(f(x)\). A constant disappears when we differentiate, so the general antiderivative, written \(\int f(x) \, dx\), includes \(+ c\), where \(c\) is any constant.
Powers
\(\int x^{n} \, dx = \frac{x^{n + 1}}{n + 1} + c\), for \(n \ne -1\). Add 1 to the power, then divide by the new power. For \(\frac{1}{x}\), \(\int \frac{1}{x} \, dx = \log_{e} |x| + c\).
Exponential
\(\int e^{kx} \, dx = \frac{1}{k} e^{kx} + c\), for \(k \ne 0\). Divide by the number \(k\) in front of \(x\).
Trig
\(\int \sin(kx) \, dx = -\frac{1}{k} \cos(kx) + c\) and \(\int \cos(kx) \, dx = \frac{1}{k} \sin(kx) + c\). Example: \(\int \cos(2x) \, dx = \frac{1}{2} \sin(2x) + c\).
final.remember: Raise the power and divide by the new power, or divide by \(k\). The general antiderivative adds \(+ c\).

a.why: Add 1 to the power to get \(x^{3}\), then divide by the new power 3: \(\frac{6x^{3}}{3} = 2x^{3}\). The option \(12x\) comes from differentiating instead: multiplying by the power and lowering it by 1. The option \(3x^{3}\) divides by the old power 2, and \(6x^{3}\) forgets to divide at all.
a.clue: Raise the power by 1, then divide by the new power.

b.why: Integrate each term. \(e^{3x}\) gives \(\frac{1}{3} e^{3x}\), and \(\sin(2x)\) gives \(-\frac{1}{2} \cos(2x)\). The sign is negative because the derivative of \(\cos x\) is \(-\sin x\), and multiplying by \(k\) instead of dividing is a common slip.
b.clue: Divide by \(k\) in each term, and check the sign for \(\sin\).
